blocks.en: 👑 Radical Ten Commandments — Unit 4: Love Neighbor
blocks.es_reference: 👑 Diez Mandamientos Radicales — Unidad 4: Ama a Tu Prójimo

blocks.en: “And the second is like it: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’” — Matthew 22:39 (NKJV)  |  citing Leviticus 19:18
blocks.es_reference: “Y el segundo es semejante a él: ‘Amarás a tu prójimo como a ti mismo.’” — Mateo 22:39 (RVG)  |  citando Levítico 19:18

blocks.en: I. Like the First — The Word Homoia
blocks.es_reference: I. Como Él — La Palabra Homoia

blocks.en: The second great commandment arrives with an astonishing qualifier. Jesus does not say “the second is almost as important,” or “the second is a close runner-up.” He says the second is homoios—“like it,” of the same kind, structurally identical in its claim on your life. There is no daylight between loving God and loving your neighbor. They form a single architecture, and Jesus refuses to let anyone inhabit one room while boarding up the other.
blocks.es_reference: El segundo gran mandamiento llega con un calificador asombroso. Jesús no dice «el segundo es casi tan importante» ni «el segundo es un finalista cercano.» Dice que el segundo es homoios—«semejante a él,» de la misma clase, estructuralmente idéntico en su demanda sobre tu vida. No hay espacio entre amar a Dios y amar al prójimo. Forman una sola arquitectura, y Jesús se niega a dejar que alguien habite una habitación mientras clausura la otra.

blocks.en: The lawyer who provoked this exchange was trying to establish a hierarchy—to find out which commandment, when followed, would exempt him from the rest. Jesus’ answer dismantled the attempt entirely. “On these two commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 22:40). Remove either one and the whole structure collapses.
blocks.es_reference: El abogado que provocó este intercambio intentaba establecer una jerarquía: averiguar qué mandamiento, si lo cumplía, lo eximiría de los demás. La respuesta de Jesús desmanteló el intento por completo. «De estos dos mandamientos dependen toda la ley y los profetas» (Mat. 22:40). Quita cualquiera de los dos y toda la estructura se derrumba.

blocks.en: The Apostle John drew the conclusion most of us would rather avoid: “If someone says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, he is a liar; for he who does not love his brother whom he has seen, how can he love God whom he has not seen?” (1 John 4:20). The proof of the vertical is in the horizontal. Love for God, if it is real, flows downhill. You cannot claim devotion to the invisible One while being indifferent to the visible one standing in front of you.
blocks.es_reference: El apóstol Juan sacó la conclusión que la mayoría preferiríamos evitar: «Si alguno dice: Yo amo a Dios, y aborrece a su hermano, es mentiroso. Pues el que no ama a su hermano a quien ha visto, ¿cómo puede amar a Dios a quien no ha visto?» (1 Jn. 4:20). La prueba de lo vertical está en lo horizontal. El amor a Dios, si es real, fluye hacia abajo. No puedes afirmar tu devoción al Invisible mientras eres indiferente al visible que está de pie frente a ti.

blocks.en: This is the cross-shaped life. The vertical beam—love for God—and the horizontal beam—love for neighbor—are not two poles pulling in opposite directions. They meet, and they hold.
blocks.es_reference: Esta es la vida en forma de cruz. El brazo vertical—amor a Dios—y el brazo horizontal—amor al prójimo—no son dos polos que tiran en direcciones opuestas. Se encuentran, y se sostienen.

blocks.en: II. Who Is My Neighbor? — Luke 10:25–29
blocks.es_reference: II. ¿Y Quién Es Mi Prójimo? — Lucas 10:25–29

blocks.en: The Pharisee’s lawyer was not satisfied. “And who is my neighbor?” he asked (Luke 10:29). Luke tells us he was “wanting to justify himself”—dikaiōsai heauton. He wanted Jesus to draw a line short enough to include his friends and long enough to exclude his inconveniences.
blocks.es_reference: El abogado fariseo no quedó satisfecho. «¿Y quién es mi prójimo?» preguntó (Lc. 10:29). Lucas nos dice que quiso «justificarse a sí mismo». Quería que Jesús trazara una línea lo suficientemente corta para incluir a sus amigos y lo suficientemente larga para excluir sus inconveniencias.

blocks.en: Jesus did not draw the line. He told a story.
blocks.es_reference: Jesús no trazó la línea. Contó una historia.

blocks.en: The road from Jerusalem to Jericho dropped seventeen miles and three thousand feet through limestone desert notorious for ambush. A man—unnamed, uncategorized—fell among thieves. He was stripped, beaten, and left half dead.
blocks.es_reference: El camino de Jerusalén a Jericó descendía diecisiete millas por desierto de piedra caliza, notorio por las emboscadas. Un hombre—sin nombre ni categoría—cayó en manos de ladrones. Fue despojado, golpeado y dejado medio muerto.

blocks.en: A priest came down the road. He passed by. A Levite came. He looked and passed by. The reasons are not given. They may have seemed good at the time—ritual purity concerns, fear of a trap, a schedule to keep, a sermon to deliver. What the text gives us is not their motivation but their trajectory: they crossed to the other side.
blocks.es_reference: Un sacerdote venía por el camino. Pasó de largo. Vino un levita. Miró y pasó de largo. Las razones no se dan. Quizás les parecieron buenas en su momento: la preocupación por la pureza ritual, el temor a una trampa, una agenda que cumplir, un sermón que predicar. Lo que el texto nos da no es su motivación sino su trayectoria: se pasaron al otro lado.

blocks.en: Then came a Samaritan. Jews and Samaritans had a centuries-old mutual contempt. This man had every cultural permission to pass. He stopped.
blocks.es_reference: Entonces vino un samaritano. Judíos y samaritanos se despreciaban mutuamente desde hacía siglos. Este hombre tenía todo el permiso cultural para seguir de largo. Se detuvo.

blocks.en: Jesus’ genius is in the question he asks at the end. He changes the lawyer’s question. The lawyer asked: “Who is my neighbor?”—meaning, who qualifies to receive my love? Jesus asks: “Which of the three was a neighbor to the man who fell among the thieves?”—meaning, who showed neighbor-love? The question shifts from category to conduct. You do not find your neighbor by drawing a circle. You become a neighbor by stopping.
blocks.es_reference: El genio de Jesús está en la pregunta que hace al final. Cambia la pregunta del abogado. El abogado preguntó: «¿Y quién es mi prójimo?»—es decir, ¿quién califica para recibir mi amor? Jesús pregunta: «¿Quién de estos tres te parece que fue el prójimo del que cayó en manos de los ladrones?»—es decir, ¿quién mostró amor al prójimo? La pregunta pasa de la categoría a la conducta. No encuentras a tu prójimo trazando un círculo. Te conviertes en prójimo deteniéndote.

blocks.en: III. The Samaritan’s Cost — Luke 10:30–35
blocks.es_reference: III. El Costo del Samaritano — Lucas 10:30–35

blocks.en: Luke’s account is remarkable for its accounting. He does not say the Samaritan “helped” in some vague, general way. He itemizes.
blocks.es_reference: El relato de Lucas es notable por su contabilidad. No dice que el samaritano «ayudó» de alguna manera vaga y general. Detalla los gastos.

blocks.en: The Samaritan came to the wounded man and bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine (v. 34)—his own medical supplies, probably packed for his own journey. He set him on his own animal—which means the Samaritan walked while the injured man rode. He brought him to an inn. He took care of him through the night. In the morning he paid the innkeeper two denarii—two days’ wages—with a commitment that went further still: “Take care of him; and whatever more you spend, when I come back, I will repay you” (v. 35). He wrote a blank check.
blocks.es_reference: El samaritano se acercó al herido y le vendó las heridas, echándoles aceite y vino (v. 34)—sus propios suministros médicos, probablemente empacados para su propio viaje. Lo montó sobre su propia caballería—lo que significa que el samaritano caminó mientras el herido cabalgaba. Lo llevó a una posada. Se ocupó de él durante la noche. Por la mañana pagó al posadero dos denarios—dos días de salario—con un compromiso que fue aún más lejos: «Cuídale; y todo lo que gastes de más, yo te lo pagaré cuando regrese» (v. 35). Firmó un cheque en blanco.

blocks.en: Count the costs: his oil, his wine, his animal’s comfort, his own feet on a seventeen-mile road, his time, his money, and an open-ended financial promise to a stranger he might never see again. This is love that is specific, costly, and named.
blocks.es_reference: Cuenta los costos: su aceite, su vino, la comodidad de su animal, sus propios pies en un camino de diecisiete millas, su tiempo, su dinero, y una promesa financiera abierta a un extraño que quizás nunca volvería a ver. Este es el amor que es específico, costoso y nombrado.

blocks.en: Sentiment is none of those things. Sentiment says, “Someone should do something about that.” The Samaritan did something. He moved toward the need, named a real cost, and committed to a real follow-through. That is what neighbor-love looks like when it stops being a principle and starts being a person.
blocks.es_reference: El sentimentalismo no es nada de eso. El sentimentalismo dice: «Alguien debería hacer algo al respecto.» El samaritano hizo algo. Se acercó a la necesidad, nombró un costo real, y se comprometió a un seguimiento real. Así es como se ve el amor al prójimo cuando deja de ser un principio y comienza a ser una persona.

blocks.en: IV. The Second Tablet — Commandments 5–10
blocks.es_reference: IV. La Segunda Tabla — Mandamientos 5–10

blocks.en: When Jesus said “Love your neighbor as yourself,” he was summarizing commandments five through ten of the Decalogue. Each of these six commandments is a fence built around your neighbor.
blocks.es_reference: Cuando Jesús dijo «Amarás a tu prójimo como a ti mismo,» estaba resumiendo los mandamientos quinto al décimo del Decálogo. Cada uno de estos seis mandamientos es una cerca construida alrededor de tu prójimo.

blocks.en:
Honor your father and your mother (the fifth)—protect the family structure that forms your neighbor.
You shall not murder (the sixth)—protect your neighbor’s life.
You shall not commit adultery (the seventh)—protect your neighbor’s marriage.
You shall not steal (the eighth)—protect your neighbor’s property.
You shall not bear false witness (the ninth)—protect your neighbor’s reputation.
You shall not covet (the tenth)—protect your neighbor’s peace.
blocks.es_reference:
Honra a tu padre y a tu madre (el quinto)—protege la estructura familiar que forma a tu prójimo.
No matarás (el sexto)—protege la vida de tu prójimo.
No cometerás adulterio (el séptimo)—protege el matrimonio de tu prójimo.
No hurtarás (el octavo)—protege la propiedad de tu prójimo.
No darás falso testimonio (el noveno)—protege la reputación de tu prójimo.
No codiciarás (el décimo)—protege la paz de tu prójimo.

blocks.en: Every negative command is a positive duty in disguise. “Do not murder” means “value life.” “Do not steal” means “honor what belongs to others.” “Do not covet” means “let your neighbor rest.”
blocks.es_reference: Todo mandamiento negativo es un deber positivo disfrazado. «No matarás» significa «valora la vida.» «No hurtarás» significa «honra lo que pertenece a otros.» «No codiciarás» significa «deja descansar a tu prójimo.»

blocks.en: Paul drew the same conclusion in Romans 13:9–10: “And if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this word: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ Love does no harm to a neighbor; therefore love is the fulfillment of the law.” The second tablet is not abolished. It is compressed into a commandment that is harder to keep, not easier. It is easier not to murder than it is to love the man who deserves to be hated.
blocks.es_reference: Pablo llegó a la misma conclusión en Romanos 13:9–10: «Y cualquier otro mandamiento, en esta sentencia se resume: Amarás a tu prójimo como a ti mismo. El amor no hace mal al prójimo; así que el cumplimiento de la ley es el amor.» La segunda tabla no está abolida. Está comprimida en un mandamiento que es más difícil de guardar, no más fácil. Es más fácil no matar que amar al hombre que merece ser odiado.

blocks.en: V. The Royal Law — James 2:8–13
blocks.es_reference: V. La Ley Real — Santiago 2:8–13

blocks.en: James 2:8 gives the commandment a title: “the royal law”—nomos basilikon in Greek—literally, the law of the King. It is not merely a rule. It is the sovereign’s edict, binding on every subject of the kingdom.
blocks.es_reference: Santiago 2:8 le da al mandamiento un título: «la ley real»—nomos basilikon en griego—literalmente, la ley del Rey. No es simplemente una regla. Es el edicto del soberano, vinculante para cada súbdito del reino.

blocks.en: James deploys this title precisely at the point where neighbor-love fails most often: partiality. “But if you show partiality, you commit sin, and are convicted by the law as transgressors” (v. 9). Partiality—prosōpolēmpsia, literally “receiving of faces”—is the practice of treating people differently based on appearance, wealth, or social position.
blocks.es_reference: Santiago despliega este título precisamente en el punto donde el amor al prójimo falla con más frecuencia: la parcialidad. «Pero si hacéis acepción de personas, cometéis pecado, y quedáis convictos por la ley como transgresores» (v. 9). La parcialidad—prosōpolēmpsia, literalmente «recibir rostros»—es la práctica de tratar a las personas de manera diferente según su apariencia, riqueza o posición social.

blocks.en: The wealthy man in fine clothing gets the good seat. The poor man is told to stand or sit on the floor (vv. 2–4). James says: you just violated the royal law. You chose a face over a commandment.
blocks.es_reference: El hombre rico con ropa fina recibe el buen asiento. Al hombre pobre se le dice que se quede de pie o que se siente en el suelo (vv. 2–4). Santiago dice: acabas de violar la ley real. Elegiste un rostro sobre un mandamiento.

blocks.en: Partiality is the easiest violation of neighbor-love to miss because it does not feel like violence. It feels like preference. But preference, when it is based on social advantage rather than real need, is the opposite of how the Good Samaritan moved. He did not ask whether the man in the ditch was worth stopping for. He saw a need and responded.
blocks.es_reference: La parcialidad es la violación del amor al prójimo más fácil de pasar por alto porque no se siente como violencia. Se siente como preferencia. Pero la preferencia, cuando se basa en la ventaja social en lugar de la necesidad real, es lo opuesto a cómo se movió el Buen Samaritano. No preguntó si valía la pena detenerse por el hombre de la zanja. Vio una necesidad y respondió.

blocks.en: The royal law does not rank people by their value. It requires you to see every face as one the King has noticed.
blocks.es_reference: La ley real no clasifica a las personas por su valor. Requiere que veas cada rostro como uno que el Rey ha notado.

blocks.en: VI. Across the Street — Application
blocks.es_reference: VI. Al Otro Lado de la Calle — Aplicación

blocks.en: Your neighbor is not a theological category. Your neighbor is whoever God has placed within reach of your hand this week.
blocks.es_reference: Tu prójimo no es una categoría teológica. Tu prójimo es quien Dios ha puesto al alcance de tu mano esta semana.

blocks.en: The Samaritan was not on a mission trip. He was traveling on ordinary business when the mission field appeared in the road. He did not go searching for someone to love; love identified itself when he rounded a curve and saw a man bleeding in the ditch.
blocks.es_reference: El samaritano no iba en un viaje misionero. Viajaba en negocios ordinarios cuando el campo misionero apareció en el camino. No fue a buscar a alguien a quien amar; el amor se identificó a sí mismo cuando dobló una curva y vio a un hombre sangrando en la zanja.

blocks.en: This is where the commandment gets practical: your neighbor is not primarily the person you choose. Your neighbor is the person you encounter. The choice is not who to love—that is already decided. The choice is whether to stop.
blocks.es_reference: Aquí es donde el mandamiento se vuelve práctico: tu prójimo no es principalmente la persona que eliges. Tu prójimo es la persona que encuentras. La elección no es a quién amar—eso ya está decidido. La elección es si te detienes.

blocks.en: The Samaritan stopped. The priest and Levite had full schedules and important destinations. They arrived where they were going. The Samaritan arrived where he was needed—and he was needed in a ditch on a dangerous road seventeen miles outside Jerusalem.
blocks.es_reference: El samaritano se detuvo. El sacerdote y el levita tenían agendas llenas y destinos importantes. Llegaron adonde iban. El samaritano llegó donde era necesario—y era necesario en una zanja, en un camino peligroso, a diecisiete millas de Jerusalén.

blocks.en: Go look for your neighbor this week. You will not have to go far. And when you find the ditch—when you come around the curve and the mission field is lying there—the only question that matters is whether you stop.
blocks.es_reference: Busca a tu prójimo esta semana. No tendrás que ir muy lejos. Y cuando encuentres la zanja—cuando des la vuelta a la curva y el campo misionero esté ahí tendido—la única pregunta que importa es si te detienes.

mc.stem: The Greek word homoia in Matthew 22:39 means:
mc.why: Correct. Homoia means "of the same kind." Jesus places both commandments on equal footing — not a hierarchy but a single architecture.

mc.stem: According to 1 John 4:20, a person who claims to love God but hates his brother is:
mc.why: Correct. John is blunt: "he is a liar." The proof of love for the invisible God is love for the visible brother.

mc.stem: In the Good Samaritan parable, who passed the wounded man first?
mc.why: Correct. The priest came first, then the Levite — both religious professionals who passed by on the other side.

mc.stem: The "royal law" of James 2:8 commands us to:
mc.why: Correct. James 2:8 identifies "love your neighbor as yourself" as the royal law — the sovereign command of the King.

mc.stem: According to James 2:9, the most common violation of the royal law is:
mc.why: Correct. James 2:9 names partiality — treating people differently based on wealth or status — as the primary way the royal law is broken.

mc.stem: Matthew 22:39 quotes which Old Testament verse?
mc.why: Correct. "Love your neighbor as yourself" comes from Leviticus 19:18 — a commandment Israel received at Sinai.

mc.stem: In the Good Samaritan parable, who ultimately helped the wounded man?
mc.why: Correct. The Samaritan — a cultural enemy of the Jews — stopped, gave first aid, transported the man, and paid for his ongoing care.

mc.stem: The commandment "You shall not murder" is:
mc.why: Correct. The sixth commandment — "You shall not murder" — guards your neighbor's life.

mc.stem: The second tablet of the Ten Commandments (5–10) primarily guards your neighbor's:
options: Life, family, property, reputation, and peace
mc.why: Correct. The second tablet is a series of protections: life (6th), marriage (7th), property (8th), reputation (9th), peace (10th) — and family structure (5th).

mc.stem: The Samaritan gave the innkeeper two denarii and also promised to:
options: Return within three days with servants
Repay any additional costs upon his return
Report the robbery to Roman authorities
mc.why: Correct. "Whatever more you spend, when I come back, I will repay you" (Luke 10:35). The Samaritan wrote a blank check for a stranger's recovery.

mc.stem: Jesus said that all the Law and the Prophets "hang on":
mc.why: Correct. Matthew 22:40 — "On these two commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets." Every command in Scripture flows from loving God and neighbor.

mc.stem: The lawyer who asked "Who is my neighbor?" wanted to:
options: Narrow and limit who he was obligated to love
Receive Jesus' commendation for his piety
Open the commandment to include foreigners
mc.why: Correct. Luke 10:29 says he asked "wanting to justify himself" — he wanted a definition narrow enough to excuse him from inconvenient neighbors.

mc.stem: According to Romans 13:10, love does no:
options: Service to those who deserve judgment
Good to those who oppose it
mc.why: Correct. Romans 13:10 — "Love does no harm to a neighbor; therefore love is the fulfillment of the law."

mc.stem: James specifically calls "love your neighbor as yourself" the:
mc.why: Correct. James 2:8 calls it the "royal law" — nomos basilikon in Greek — the sovereign command of the King.

mc.stem: The Greek word basilikon in James 2:8 means:
mc.why: Correct. Basilikon comes from basileus (king). The royal law is the king's law — sovereign, not optional.

mc.stem: Jesus changed the lawyer's question from "Who is my neighbor?" to:
mc.why: Correct. Jesus asked: "Which of the three was a neighbor to the man?" He shifted from category (who qualifies) to conduct (who showed love).

mc.stem: The commandment "You shall not covet" primarily protects your neighbor's:
mc.why: Correct. The tenth commandment guards your neighbor's peace. Covetousness is the root from which murder, adultery, theft, and false witness grow.

mc.stem: In addition to two denarii, the Samaritan's final commitment to the innkeeper was:
options: A letter of commendation to city officials
An open-ended pledge to repay whatever more was spent
Payment of the wounded man's travel expenses
Three days of personal nursing care
mc.why: Correct. "Whatever more you spend, when I come back, I will repay you" — the Samaritan wrote a blank check for a stranger's recovery.

mc.stem: According to 1 John 4:20, love for God is ultimately proved by:
mc.why: Correct. "He who does not love his brother whom he has seen, how can he love God whom he has not seen?" The horizontal is the test of the vertical.

mc.stem: According to Romans 13:9–10, all the commandments are summed up in:
mc.why: Correct. Romans 13:9 — "if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this word: You shall love your neighbor as yourself."

fill.prompt: Jesus calls the second commandment ____, the Greek word for "like it," of the same kind as the first.
On these two commandments hang all the Law and the ____ (Matt. 22:40).
Because love for God flows downhill, the proof of the vertical is in the ____.
Luke says the lawyer asked "Who is my neighbor?" because he was wanting to ____ himself.
The man fell among thieves on the dangerous road from Jerusalem to ____.
In the morning the Samaritan paid the innkeeper two ____, two days' wages.
Jesus' closing question shifts the lawyer's question from category to ____.
Commandments five through ten, which "Love your neighbor as yourself" summarizes, make up the second ____.
James 2:8 calls love of neighbor "the ____ law," literally the law of the King.
James says neighbor-love fails most often at the point of ____: treating people differently by appearance, wealth, or social position.

sa.prompt: Explain why Jesus uses the word homoia ("like it") in Matthew 22:39 and what this teaches about the relationship between loving God and loving neighbor.
sa.model: Homoia means "of the same kind" — not second in importance but equal in structural claim on the disciple's life. The two commandments form a cross: vertical (love God) and horizontal (love neighbor). 1 John 4:20 shows they cannot be separated: claiming love for God while failing the visible neighbor is a self-contradiction.

sa.prompt: Re-narrate the Good Samaritan parable (Luke 10:30–35) and explain what each specific cost the Samaritan paid teaches about the nature of neighbor-love.
sa.model: The Samaritan gave his medical supplies (oil and wine), his animal's comfort (walking so the injured man could ride), his time (stayed overnight), two denarii, and an open-ended pledge. Each item shows neighbor-love is specific, costly, and committed — not vague sentiment.

sa.prompt: List the six commandments of the Second Tablet (5–10) and explain how each one protects your neighbor.
sa.model: The fifth guards family structure, the sixth guards life, the seventh guards marriage, the eighth guards property, the ninth guards reputation, the tenth guards peace. Romans 13:10 — "love does no harm to a neighbor; therefore love is the fulfillment of the law." Each negative command is a positive duty.

sa.prompt: Apply Romans 13:9–10 to a specific situation in ministry or daily life, showing how the second-tablet commandments are expressions of neighbor-love.
sa.model: Romans 13:9-10 summarizes the second tablet in love: "love does no harm to a neighbor; therefore love is the fulfillment of the law." Any contemporary situation (business dealings, speech, family relations) can be tested: does this action harm my neighbor? If yes, love forbids it.

sa.prompt: Define partiality as James describes it in James 2:1–9 and give two examples of how partiality shows up in the modern church.
sa.model: Partiality (prosōpolēmpsia — "receiving of faces") is treating people differently based on wealth, status, or appearance. James illustrates it with the wealthy man getting the good seat while the poor man is told to stand. Modern examples include favoring generous donors in decisions or giving more pastoral care to influential families.

sa.prompt: Use 1 John 4:20 to examine the claim "I love God." What does John say is the proof of that claim, and why does the visible/invisible distinction matter?
sa.model: John says the person who claims to love God while hating the visible brother "is a liar." The argument runs from lesser to greater: if you cannot love the neighbor you can see and touch, you cannot love the God you cannot see. Love for God must pass the visible test.

sa.prompt: Explain how Jesus changed the lawyer's question in Luke 10:25–37, and what this change reveals about the nature of neighbor-love.
sa.model: The lawyer asked "Who is my neighbor?" seeking to narrow obligation. Jesus changed it to "Who became a neighbor?" — shifting from category (who deserves love) to conduct (who showed love). Neighbor-love is not about finding eligible recipients; it is about becoming the kind of person who stops.

sa.prompt: What does the behavior of the priest and Levite in the parable reveal about the relationship between religious function and genuine neighbor-love?
sa.model: The priest and Levite were the most religiously qualified people in Israel — yet they passed by. Jesus chose these characters deliberately: religious function does not guarantee neighbor-love. Ritual, schedule, and purity concerns can become excuses for avoiding the costly demand of the person in the ditch.

sa.prompt: How does Section VI ("Across the Street") apply the Good Samaritan parable to ordinary daily life? Distinguish between seeking a neighbor and encountering one.
sa.model: The Samaritan was not on a mission trip — he was traveling on ordinary business. The "mission field" appeared in the road. Neighbor-love is primarily reactive to real encounters, not proactive searches for worthy recipients. The choice is not who to love but whether to stop when love is needed.

sa.prompt: Connect Unit 4 (Love Neighbor) to Unit 5 (Be Holy): why does loving your neighbor at the level Jesus demands require more than effort alone?
sa.model: The Samaritan's love cost him everything on the road that day. Sustaining that kind of love across a lifetime — toward enemies, the ungrateful, the difficult — cannot be powered by human will alone. It requires the Spirit's transforming work. Holiness is the only engine powerful enough to sustain radical neighbor-love.
